title: Clay jars (2 Corinthians 4:7–9)
hookLine: treasure in clay jars: pressed but not crushed

lines: A SAFE, A VAULT, A VELVET BOX.
OR THE CHIPPED MUG BY THE SINK.
cards: Where would you keep something priceless? A safe. A vault.
A velvet box with a lock. Not, probably, in the chipped mug by the sink. And yet that's where Paul says God keeps it.
Same letter as yesterday's list, a few chapters earlier. Paul has been talking about light, and faces, and what God has put inside ordinary people.
Then he reaches for the plainest object in any house, the clay pot that cracks if you drop it, and says: that's us.

teach.b: First, the treasure, in the King James words: "For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts."
Some readers hear an echo of let there be light: the God who lit the world has lit something inside people.
Then the jar: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us." Earthen vessels. Clay jars.
Paul doesn't pretend the jar is strong. The weakness is the point: if the jar is ordinary, nobody mistakes where the light comes from.
Then life in a clay jar, in four pairs: "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed."

teach.h: A BLOW, AND THEN A BUT NOT.
teach.b: Each pair has the same shape: a blow, and then a but not. In plainer words, pressed, but not crushed. Knocked down, but not finished.
Paul never says the blows don't land. They do. They just don't get the last inch.
Some readers hear an echo of Gideon in Judges, whose small band carried empty pitchers with lamps hidden inside; at the signal they broke the pitchers, and the light shone out in the dark.
Paul doesn't mention Gideon, so that's a connection readers make. But it fits. A clay jar isn't a failure of the treasure.

how: Some Christians return to the clay jars passage in times of illness, burnout or loss, and some churches and ministries use a clay jar or a broken pot with a light inside as a picture of God's power in human weakness.

o: the jars of oil used to anoint kings in the Bible
ordinary, breakable people carrying God's light inside
a warning that weak people can't carry God's power

s: in Paul's picture, the treasure in the jars is gold
the treasure is light: God "hath shined in our hearts."
Paul says the jars are clay so the power is seen to be God's
"that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us."
Paul says believers never get knocked down
he says "cast down, but not destroyed." the blows land; they don't finish.

games.q: you're with Gideon's small band at night. each of you holds a trumpet and an empty pitcher with a lamp hidden inside. the signal comes. what do you do with the pitcher?
o: keep it whole so the light stays hidden.
break it, so the lamp shines out.
games.why: they break the pitchers and the lamps shine in the dark. Paul never mentions Gideon, but some readers hear the echo in the clay jars.

practice: If there's a mug or a bowl near you, pick it up, or cup your empty hands, and feel how plain it is: the chip, the stain, the crack in the glaze.

Think of yourself the way Paul thinks of the jar, not polished, not unbreakable, still carrying something, and name one place you feel pressed right now, then quietly say the other half: but not crushed.
If you pray, you can thank God for the light in an ordinary jar.

wordCard.voice: Clay jars. Paul's picture of ordinary, breakable people carrying God's light, so the power is plainly God's. Troubled, but not distressed.

orig.note: Greek: in clay vessels, Paul's phrase in 2 Corinthians 4:7 (KJV: earthen vessels).

carryVoice: Your line: pressed, not crushed. In Paul's picture, the cracks don't disqualify the jar. Go gently.
